episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Does a place still exist if nobody records it?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Fast Company] I use AI to save time. So why am I working more? and [Engadget] Why is it illegal to use a Bluetooth jammer?, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: How should small rural venues document and share their performances in ways that preserve context and serve community rather than extracting value for external platforms? Topics include: Platform extraction of value from local cultural recordings without attribution or benefit to source communities, Cost barriers to rural venues accessing professional stage production and documentation technology, The difference between existence and legibility of places in digital systems, Technology adoption failures in volunteer-run venues lacking dedicated staff and IT infrastructure, Physical documentation (programs, instruments with provenance) versus digital files as preservation methods.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Museum of the Cariboo Chilcotin

discussion.central_question: How should small rural venues document and share their performances in ways that preserve context and serve community rather than extracting value for external platforms?
discussion.riley_position: Digital tools can democratize documentation and reach if venues treat recording as standing infrastructure rather than one-off novelty projects, and if venues control their own recordings to keep contextual information attached.
riley_key_evidence: A hobbyist built a 512-LED stage lighting matrix from a modded Nintendo Switch and ESP32 board for a fraction of commercial equipment rental costs
The Earth Garden platform strips field recordings of context and credit, making a Horsefly creek recording indistinguishable from any other ambient audio globally
The Randy Bachman guitar reunion succeeded through physical documentation and people who cared, not through recording technology
discussion.casey_position: Technology adoption in rural venues fails because it ignores capacity constraints and governance questions; external platforms extract value without providing measurable benefit to places, and digital documentation doesn't automatically survive unless deliberate systems preserve context.
casey_key_evidence: Digital ID verification apps at UK venues created longer lines rather than shorter ones, a problem that rural volunteer-run halls couldn't staff to manage
Earth Garden recordings provide no credit line or search traffic benefit back to the place where the recording was made
Even with a recorded file, someone must actively maintain and govern what gets kept versus deleted as storage fills up over time
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey reached partial agreement that venues owning their own recording equipment and treating it as a standing job description (not a grant-dependent novelty) is a realistic lower-floor solution, though Casey notes this still requires governance decisions about long-term data management that technology alone cannot solve.
